research.summary:
BOTTOM LINE: The evidence does not back bankruptcy filing counts (Epiq or US Courts totals, consumer or business) as an early-warning signal. Against unemployment and recessions they move at the same time or later. Changes in the law swamp them, and they fell during the 1981-82, 2001 and 2020 recessions. One bankruptcy-related series did lead: the dollar value of liabilities in business failures, which is driven by larger firms (NBER data for 1879-1938: average lead of 10.5 months at peaks; median lead of 7 months over 43 turning points). But its leads were long and erratic (26-28 months before the 1953 and 1957 peaks). It stopped working after 1948 and was dropped from the leading short list in 1966. Simple counts of failures, mostly small firms, moved roughly with the cycle. Casey's 'pre-cog' instinct is right about the size-weighted, large-firm part of distress and wrong about headline counts.

LEAD/LAG BY TARGET:
(a) Recessions (NBER peaks). Leading but erratic and fading: failure liabilities and large-firm failures. Coincident: counts of failures. Coincident or lagging: personal filings. Mixed: corporate default rates. They rose before 1990 and 2001 but sat near record lows before 2008 and 2020, and rose in 1986 and 2016 with no recession following.
(b) Unemployment. Filings move with it (correlation 0.42-0.54 after removing trend) and peak after it does: NY Fed new bankruptcy notations peaked in 2010Q2, unemployment in Oct 2009. Jobless claims lead (median 6 months). Epiq's own head called filings 'largely a lagging economic indicator'.
(c) Stock bear markets. The evidence runs the other way: stock returns and volatility forecast default rates and firm failures. No rigorous study shows filings predicting market drawdowns.
(d) Credit spreads and default waves. Over 1866-2008, lagged spreads did not forecast default rates. Default rates persist and peak in or after recessions. The predictive power of spreads for the economy sits in the excess bond premium, not in expected defaults (in-sample result). The claim that the HY distress ratio leads defaults is contested.

CONTAGION (Casey's mechanism): real, but local, industry-specific, small on average and slow.
- Rivals and creditors lose about 0.4% to 2.3% of value.
- Suppliers are hit, and the hit starts before the filing.
- When a business is liquidated, other employers on the same Census block lose about 4% of jobs per year over 5 years (about 1.3 extra jobs lost per job lost), mostly where the neighbours were already weak.
- The big second-round effects came through foreclosures and household leverage in 2007-09, amplified by banks and collateral. Corporate bond default crises had no significant effect on output. Consumer-bankruptcy debt relief raised employment by about 2% in 2007-10: the filing is often the shock absorber.
- No study shows local filings leading local job losses. The state-panel evidence runs from labor-market recessions to filings.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR ALERTS:
1. Do not alert on total filings. Show them as a confirmation and severity panel: per capita, detrended, with flags for legal breaks (2005 bankruptcy reform, COVID, the Subchapter V debt limit; Senate bill S.3977 passed Aug 3 2026 and is pending).
2. If any bankruptcy series gets an alert, pre-register an out-of-sample test of the size-weighted large-firm measure and how widely it spreads across sectors. Expect long, variable leads and false alarms: 1986, 2016, and 2023-26 so far (785 large filings in 2025 per S&P, with no NBER-dated peak yet).
3. Use flows, not stocks: new transitions into delinquency by loan type and state. The NY Fed showed in Aug 2026 that the stock of 90+ day card delinquency is inflated by charged-off debt that stays on credit reports. The one modern case where household distress clearly led (subprime mortgages from mid-2005) was confined to one segment.
4. The signals that do lead are already mostly on the dashboard: market pricing and credit supply (stock drawdowns and volatility, excess bond premium and HY spreads, loan officer tightening) and the credit boom itself (credit-market sentiment, household debt growth). What bankruptcies add is a map of where stress is concentrated and a severity read.
5. Statistical power is low: about 7 recessions, mostly in-sample results, and the classic failure-liabilities lead itself failed out of sample after 1948.

CURRENT READ (Oct 2026): Epiq filings are up 11% year-to-date, but from a low base: NY Fed new bankruptcy notations were 137k in 2026Q2, about a third below the 2019 average. Large-company filings have run at 16-year highs for about three years. Flow delinquency is flat for cards and up slightly for auto and mortgages. That confirms softness; it does not show an accelerating wave.

Two notes: the AER paper by Fay, Hurst and White is from 2002, not 1998 (1998 was the working paper). Epiq's Oct 2026 release says individual filings rose 7%, but its own counts imply 11.2%.

findings.claim: [Classic 1938] Mitchell & Burns put total liabilities of business failures (inverted) on their list of the 21 most trustworthy indicators of revivals. Average lead: 9 months, measured at troughs only.
findings.evidence: NBER Bulletin 69 (1938), reprinted as Moore (1961) ch. 6. Series: Bradstreet's total liabilities of failures, inverted. Average lead 9 months. Covers 12 business cycles and 14 revivals: 13 leads, 1 lag, range -17 to +6 months. Erratic movements 'pronounced'. Lagged by 6 months at the 1901 revival. Bradstreet's compilation was discontinued in January 1933. Only revivals (troughs) were studied, not peaks.

findings.claim: [Classic 1950] Moore's 1950 list counted failure liabilities (inverted) among 8 leading series. Average lead was 10.5 months at peaks and 7.5 months at troughs over 1879-1938.
findings.evidence:
Moore (1950), NBER Occasional Paper 31, reprinted as Moore (1961) ch. 7.
- Table 7.11 (Dun's, 1879-1938). Peaks: 14 turns, 11 leads, average -10.5 months. Troughs: 16 turns, 14 leads, average -7.5 months.
- Table 7.1, peaks before 1937: range -23 to +2, average -8. May 1937 peak: -4.
- Postwar: inverted liabilities peaked in April 1945, about 43 months before the Nov 1948 business peak.

findings.claim: [Classic 1961] The lead comes from large firms and dollar-weighted liabilities. Simple counts of failures, mostly small firms, are roughly coincident. Postwar leads were very long and erratic.
findings.evidence:
Zarnowitz & Lerner (1961), Table 12.2, 1879-1938, inverted series:
- Liabilities: -10.5 months at peaks (average deviation 8.0), -7.5 at troughs.
- Number of failures: -5.0 at peaks with 5 lags out of 14 (average deviation 6.8); -0.5 at troughs.
- Trading-company counts (small firms): -0.4 at peaks, +1.4 at troughs.
- Large manufacturing failures (liabilities of $100k or more): -5.1 at peaks, -6.9 at troughs; anticipated 16 of 21 turns.
Postwar: liabilities led the July 1953 peak by 28 months and the July 1957 peak by 26 months; 0 months at the Apr 1958 trough. Counts skipped the 1953-54 cycle.
Mechanism: failure liabilities track the share of firms with falling profits (profit diffusion). Failures are a symptom of an earlier, broad profit squeeze.

findings.claim: [Classic, dropped] Failure liabilities were dropped from the leading short list in 1966 because they stopped working after 1948. No failure or bankruptcy series has been in the leading index since 1987.
findings.evidence:
Moore & Shiskin (1967), Business Conditions Digest series 14, liabilities (inverted):
- Total score 68: conformity 86, timing 66, smoothness 0.
- Since 1879: 43 turns, 31 leads, 3 lags, median lead -7 months.
- 1960-list record at peaks: -28 to +3 (median -7); -12 at the May 1960 peak; no matching turn at the Feb 1961 trough.
- Reason for dropping it: 'poor timing and conformity record since 1948'. Since 1950 its movements were obscured by irregular swings and a strong upward trend.
Afterwards:
- Failure counts entered the 1975 leading index only inside the net business formation index (BCD May 1975). That index was suspended in March 1987 because one component was of poor quality and another's data was unavailable in time (Zarnowitz 1992, Table 11.5, notes aa and k).
- The Jan 1989 BCD still charted series 14 under 'credit difficulties', but the revised index added no failure series.
- The D&B annual series in Historical Statistics of the US ends in 1998.
- Today's Conference Board leading index and its six-part Leading Credit Index (swap spread, LIBOR-bill spread, margin debt, AAII sentiment, loan officer survey, repo liabilities) contain no failure or default series.
findings.confidence: verified-primary (the 1998 end date of the D&B series is secondary)

findings.claim: [Classic, comparison] In the same 1966 scoring, jobless claims and installment-loan delinquency led with shorter but cleaner leads. The 1950 leading group as a whole held up after the war.
findings.evidence:
Moore & Shiskin (1967):
- Initial jobless claims (inverted), from 1945: score 73; 10 turns; 6 leads; 1 lag; median lead -6 months.
- Installment-loan delinquency (inverted), from 1948: score 59; 8 turns; 6 leads; 2 lags; median lead -3 months.
Moore (1979), as summarised in Zarnowitz (1992) Table 10.6: the 1950 leading group (which included failure liabilities) averaged a 12-month lead at peaks over 1948-75, versus 6 months through 1938. That is group-level evidence only.

findings.claim: [Personal bankruptcy, cycle] In a state panel, personal bankruptcy rates rise throughout labor-market recessions and peak after they end. Recessions explain only about two-fifths of the rise; trend and legal factors dominate.
findings.evidence:
Garrett & Wall (Macroeconomic Dynamics 2014; MPRA 42740). 45 states, 1988Q1-2004Q4, 3,105 observations. State labor-market recessions dated with a Markov-switching model on Philadelphia Fed coincident indexes.
- Bankruptcy rate above trend by 6.4 per 100k after year 1 and 12.4 by year 3.
- After a 1-year recession, the rate peaks about 6.8 above trend in the 2nd quarter of recovery, then falls below trend.
- Recessions accounted for 12.6 of a 31.6-point rise.
- The national rate fell during 2 of the 5 NBER recessions in 1980-2009 (the early-1980s one, written '1982-83' in the paper, and 2001).
- The paper cites Fay et al. (2002), White (2009) and Fisher (2005) as finding filing decisions unrelated to local unemployment.

findings.claim: [Personal bankruptcy, COVID] Before 2020, filings and unemployment moved together within the same quarter. In 2020 the link reversed: filings fell 31% during the worst job loss since the Depression.
findings.evidence:
Wang, Yang, Iverson & Jiang (Mar 2021):
- Detrended filings vs unemployment: correlation 0.42 (0.54 excluding 2005); 'largely contemporaneous at the quarterly level'.
- 2020 vs 2019: total filings -31%; Chapter 7 about -25%; Chapter 13 about -55%.
- Q2 2020: the historical relation implied 200k+ extra consumer filings; actual was 81k fewer. Business filings: about 5,500 more expected, 645 fewer actual.
- States with larger unemployment increases saw larger filing declines.
- Drivers: forbearance, stimulus, liquidity constraints.

findings.claim: [Personal bankruptcy, lag statements] A Fed regional note and the largest filings-data vendor both describe filings as lagging the economy.
findings.evidence:
Chicago Fed Letter 52 (Eugeni 1991):
- Filings 'sometimes respond to recessions with a lag'; laid-off workers 'do not file for bankruptcy immediately'.
- National filings rose 20% in 1985 and 32% in 1986 with no national recession, driven by regional busts. New England filings rose about 65% in its 1989-90 slump.
Epiq AACER (Chris Kruse, May 7 2020): filings data are 'largely a lagging economic indicator'; 'filings start to increase several months after the economy turns'.

findings.claim: [Personal bankruptcy, legal breaks and lag in credit-report data] Legal changes dwarf the cycle. Consumer bankruptcies peaked after unemployment peaked and remain well below 2019 levels.
findings.evidence:
National rate, per 1,000 people (Garrett & Wall): 0.3 in 1985Q1 rising to 1.2 in 2004Q4. Bankruptcy-reform rush: 2.2 in 2005Q4, then 0.4 in 2006Q1.
NY Fed Consumer Credit Panel, new bankruptcy notations (thousands per quarter; sheet 'Page 17 Data'):
- 949 in 2005Q4, then 214 in 2006Q1.
- Rose from 259 to 352 during 2007, partly a mechanical rebound after the reform.
- Peaked at 621 in 2010Q2, about 8 months after unemployment peaked at 10.0% in Oct 2009 (FRED UNRATE).
- 94-136 in 2020-22.
- 137 in 2026Q2, about 1/3 below the 2019 quarterly average of about 204.
Citation fix: Fay, Hurst & White is AER 2002, 92(3):706-718. The 1998 item is the U. Michigan working paper 'The Bankruptcy Decision: Does Stigma Matter?'. Its full text is paywalled; its finding is cited here via Garrett & Wall.
findings.confidence: verified-primary (the Fay-Hurst-White finding itself is secondary)

findings.claim: [Corporate defaults, 150 years] Default cycles are persistent and only loosely tied to recessions. Stock prices and volatility forecast defaults; credit spreads do not.
findings.evidence:
Giesecke, Longstaff, Schaefer & Strebulaev (NBER w15848; JFE 2011). Value-weighted bond defaults, 1866-2008.
- 13 default cycles vs 31 NBER recessions. Average length 3.2 years vs 1.5.
- Persistence (first-order autocorrelation): 0.574 for default cycles vs 0.267 for recessions.
- Correlation between the recession and default-cycle indicators: only 0.263.
- Lagged credit spreads have no predictive power for default rates.
- Lagged stock returns (negative) and stock volatility (positive) do predict defaults.
- A lagged recession indicator is significant only at 10% and drops out in the combined model.
- Spreads are about twice expected losses (about an 80bp premium) and do not respond to realized defaults.

findings.claim: [Corporate defaults, modern timing] Junk-bond default rates rose before the 1990 and 2001 recessions, but sat near record lows before 2008 and 2020. Rises in 1986 and 2016 produced no recession. The Conference Board says default rates lag the cycle.
findings.evidence:
Moody's 1920-2006 study, Exhibit 21, annual speculative-grade default rates:
- 1988: 3.6%; 1989: 5.8%; 1990: 10.1%; 1991: 10.4%.
- 1998: 3.5%; 1999: 5.8%; 2000: 6.3%; 2001: 10.6%; 2002: 8.3%.
- 1986: 5.6%, with no recession.
- 2006: 1.57%, the lowest since 1981.
Conference Board (2011): corporate spreads ranked low 'because they were lagging rather than leading... highly correlated with default rates, which tend to lag the business cycle'.
Secondary (not opened):
- 2016: 162 defaults worldwide (S&P), 66 in energy, the most since 2009, with no US recession following (Funds Europe).
- Global 12-month default rate peaked in late 2009 at about 12-13% (press coverage, after the June 2009 trough).
Verified side note: in Jan 2009, 13 months into the recession, Moody's raised its peak forecast from 10% to 15.4% within a month (Bond Vigilantes blog).
findings.confidence: verified-primary for the Moody's annual figures and the Conference Board quote; secondary for 2009 and 2016

findings.claim: [Large-company bankruptcies before 2001, 2008 and 2020] They led into 2001, were coincident in 2008, and gave no warning in 2020. Since 2023 they have been elevated with no recession dated yet.
findings.evidence:
- 2001: public-company bankruptcies began rising around 1997 while total business bankruptcies were falling. 176 in 2000 (a record at the time), 257 in 2001 (+46%), concentrated in telecom and energy and in larger, more indebted firms (FDIC FYI, Jan 2002). This echoes the large-firm lead in Zarnowitz & Lerner.
- 2008: 78 in 2007, then 136 in 2008 (+74%); 2001 later restated to 263 (AP/BankruptcyData, Jan 2009). 2006 was a low of 66 (secondary).
- 2020: S&P GMI counted 579 in 2019 and 630 in 2020, later revised to 518. An external shock, not a signal.
- Now (S&P GMI, secondary): 785 in 2025, the most since 828 in 2010; 372 in H1 2026 vs 371 in H1 2025.
- The NBER's latest dated peak is still Feb 2020 (BCDC page checked today); the committee dates turns with long lags. Whether 2023-26 is a long lead or a false alarm is unresolved.
findings.confidence: verified-primary for FDIC and NBER; secondary for the BankruptcyData figures reported by AP and for the S&P GMI counts (S&P site returned 403)

findings.claim: [Spreads vs defaults as predictors] Credit spreads predict economic activity mainly through the excess bond premium, not through expected defaults. These are in-sample results.
findings.evidence:
Gilchrist & Zakrajšek (NBER w17021; AER 2012), 1973:M1-2010:M9.
- A 100bp rise in the GZ spread means about 3pp (annualized) lower industrial production growth over the next 3 months and more than 1.25pp lower GDP growth over the next 4 quarters.
- The Baa-Aaa spread's predictive power is 'economically negligible' at one year.
- 12-month unemployment, standardized coefficients: excess bond premium 0.414 vs predicted-default spread 0.213.
- Not inconsistent with the Aug-2026 referee's rejection of the excess bond premium as a cycle-analog dimension, which was an out-of-sample test.

findings.claim: [The boom comes first] The earliest documented signals are credit exuberance before the bust, not realized distress.
findings.evidence:
- López-Salido, Stein & Zakrajšek (NBER w21879; QJE 2017), 1929-2013: elevated credit-market sentiment in year t-2 predicts lower activity in t and t+1, through predictable spread widening.
- Mian, Sufi & Verner (NBER w21581), 30 countries, 1960-2012: a medium-run rise in household debt/GDP predicts lower growth and higher unemployment.
- Lown, Morgan & Rohatgi (FRBNY EPR 2000): 'four of the past five recessions were preceded by sharply tighter standards' in the loan officer survey; the exception was 1981-82.

findings.claim: [Recession-risk research uses no bankruptcy series] Fed recession-risk work relies on unemployment, inflation and spreads, and stresses small samples.
findings.evidence:
Kiley (FEDS Note, June 2022), 1965-2019, only 7 large-unemployment-increase episodes:
- Beyond 4 quarters, unemployment and inflation predict recession risk better than financial variables.
- The Baa spread is small and borderline at 4 quarters and insignificant at 8.
- Composite leading indicators help only up to about 12 months.
The Fed recession-prediction indicator set seen via search (FEDS 2023-008) also has no bankruptcy series; that paper was not opened.

findings.claim: [Delinquency: flows, not stocks] The one modern case where household distress clearly led was confined to one segment and visible in delinquency flows. Stock-based delinquency rates can mislead.
findings.evidence:
Mayer, Pence & Sherlund (FEDS 2008-59):
- Mortgage trouble began in mid-2005.
- Subprime serious delinquency: 5.6% in mid-2005, over 21% by July 2008.
- All-loan serious delinquency: average 1.7% over 1979-2006, 4.5% by Q2 2008.
- Foreclosure starts in H1 2008: 1.2 million (+79%).
NY Fed consumer panel: new foreclosures rose from 220k (2006Q4) to 349k (2007Q4), before the Dec 2007 peak. Over the same period, bankruptcies were depressed after the 2005 reform and corporate defaults were at record lows.
Liberty Street Economics (Aug 11 2026):
- The stock of card balances 90+ days late rose from 7.6% (2022Q3) to 12.8% (2026Q1), mainly because charged-off debt stays on credit reports longer: about 40% still reported after 1 year in 2004-12, about 80% in 2024.
- The flow into 90+ 'has remained relatively stable for almost two years'.
NY Fed household debt report, 2026Q2: early-delinquency transitions up slightly for auto and mortgages, steady for cards; serious-delinquency transitions unchanged.

findings.claim: [Contagion: rivals, creditors, suppliers] Spillovers from a bankruptcy are real but specific to the industry or counterparty, small on average, and largely priced before or at the filing.
findings.evidence:
- Lang & Stulz (JFE 1992): a bankruptcy announcement lowers a value-weighted portfolio of competitors by about 1% on average. Larger in highly indebted industries; positive (rivals gain) in concentrated, low-debt industries.
- Jorion & Zhang (JFE 2007): Chapter 11 filings spread to rivals (their CDS spreads widen); Chapter 7 filings help rivals. Same-industry 11-day return: -0.41%.
- Jorion & Zhang (JF 2009; FDIC working paper 2008-08), 251 bankruptcies 1999-2005: creditors' abnormal stock returns were -0.90% over 3 days and -1.90% over 11 days; industrial creditors -2.29%, financial creditors -0.34%. Average exposure about 0.3% of equity. Creditors were more likely to become distressed later: the literal 'someone else blows up next' channel, documented firm by firm.
- Hertzel, Li, Officer & Rodgers (JFE 2008): significant losses for suppliers that begin before the filing and grow with industry contagion.
findings.confidence: Jorion & Zhang 2009: verified-primary. Lang & Stulz abstract: verified via a mirror. Jorion & Zhang 2007 and Hertzel et al.: secondary (abstract summaries).

findings.claim: [Contagion: local real effects] Second-round local damage is real, but slow, very local, concentrated where neighbours were already weak, and mostly runs through foreclosures and household leverage.
findings.evidence:
- Bernstein, Colonnelli, Giroud & Iverson (NBER w23162; JFE 2019), using random judge assignment: liquidation (vs reorganization) cuts employment at other businesses in the same Census block by about 4% per year over 5 years, about 1.3 extra jobs lost per job lost. The effect fades at larger areas and is concentrated in services and other local-market businesses.
- Benmelech et al. (NBER w20254; RFS 2019), stores 2005-09: a liquidating chain store at the same address raises neighbours' closure probability by 0.36pp (5.9% of the mean). Stores of less profitable parents (25th percentile) are 16.9-22.2% more likely to close; no significant effect at the 75th percentile.
- Mian, Sufi & Trebbi (NBER w16685): foreclosures explain 20-30% of the 2007-09 fall in house prices, 15-25% of the fall in residential investment and 20-35% of the fall in auto sales.
- Mian & Sufi (NBER w17830): household balance-sheet shocks in high-debt counties account for about 4 million (65%) of 2007-09 job losses.

findings.claim: [Contagion: limits] Corporate default waves alone barely move output; banks do the amplifying. Consumer-bankruptcy relief supported jobs rather than destroying them.
findings.evidence:
- Giesecke et al. (NBER w17854; JFE 2014), 1866-2010: corporate bond default crises (20-50% of bonds defaulting) had no significant effect on GDP or industrial production. Banking crises had long-lasting effects. Bank lending rose after default crises as borrowers switched lenders.
- Auclert, Dobbie & Goldsmith-Pinkham (NBER w25685): states with more generous bankruptcy exemptions lost fewer local-market jobs in 2007-10. Consumer-bankruptcy debt relief raised total employment by almost 2%.

findings.claim: [Regional panels] No study found shows rising local bankruptcy filings preceding local job losses. The evidence runs from labor-market recessions to filings.
findings.evidence:
- Garrett & Wall: state bankruptcy rates respond to state labor-market recessions and peak in the recovery.
- Eugeni (1991): state filings surged in states already in downturns.
- Wang et al.: unemployment and filings moved together across states in 2007-09, in opposite directions in 2020.
- Searches for state-panel causality or VAR tests of filings leading unemployment returned nothing. That is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.
findings.confidence: verified-primary for the direction; the 'no study found' result is search-based (moderate)

findings.claim: [Stock bear markets] Stock markets lead failures and defaults, not the reverse. No rigorous evidence shows aggregate filings predicting drawdowns.
findings.evidence:
- Giesecke et al.: lagged stock returns and volatility forecast default rates.
- Campbell, Hilscher & Szilagyi (NBER w12362), 1963-2003: low past returns, high volatility and low market value predict firm failure, and their model 'captures much of the time variation in the aggregate failure rate'.
- An informal regression of annual business bankruptcies on next-year market returns (1981-2003, 23 observations) found an R-squared of 0.031 and a t-statistic of 0.82 (dailyspeculations.com; not opened).
findings.confidence: verified-primary (Giesecke et al., Campbell et al.); unverified (informal regression)

findings.claim: [Practitioners: Epiq Oct 2026] The source of the 11% headline frames filings as a result of stress that is already visible and makes no leading-indicator claim. Its own figures contain an arithmetic slip.
findings.evidence:
Epiq AACER, Oct 9 2026, first nine months of 2026 vs 2025:
- Total: 469,719 (+11%).
- Chapter 7: 282,413 (+13%). Chapter 13: 160,817 (+8%).
- Commercial: 25,467 (+7%). Commercial Chapter 11: 6,560 (+11%). Subchapter V: 2,442 (+46%).
- September alone: commercial Chapter 11 was 648, -16% year on year.
Epiq (M. Hunter) cites borrowing costs, household expenses, delinquencies and a softer job market, and expects filings to keep rising into 2027. ABI (A. Quackenboss) cites inflation, borrowing costs and uncertainty.
Data check: the release says individual filings rose 7%, but its own counts (444,252 vs 399,379) imply +11.2%.
findings.confidence: verified-primary (release as reprinted by ABF Journal)

findings.claim: [Practitioners: distress ratio] The claim that the high-yield distress ratio leads defaults by 6-12 months is contested.
findings.evidence:
- Guggenheim (July 2024), seen only in a search snippet (the page now returns 404): high-yield distress ratio leads defaults by about 9-12 months (R-squared 74% since 1997); for loans the best fit is a 6-month lead (R-squared 46%).
- FTI Consulting (Eisenband, Apr 4 2024): the distress ratio 'tends to move in tandem with corporate defaults without an obvious lead–lag relationship'. Trailing 12-month default rates distort lead and lag. The correlation 'has broken down in the last year', with the distress ratio near 6% while defaults stayed high: the widest gap in 25 years.

findings.claim: [Breaks to flag in any bankruptcy series] Legal and data-definition changes repeatedly create jumps larger than cyclical signals. One is pending now.
findings.evidence:
- 2005 bankruptcy reform (BAPCPA): rush in late 2005, collapse in 2006.
- COVID forbearance and stimulus, 2020-21.
- Subchapter V: the higher debt limit expired in June 2024; the limit is now $3,424,000. Senate bill S.3977 ('Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026') passed unanimously on Aug 3 2026 to restore $7.5M permanently. The House companion H.R.7730 left committee in March 2026. Enactment and any retroactivity are unconfirmed. If enacted, small-business Chapter 11 counts would jump mechanically.
- D&B coverage expanded in 1939-40.
- Net business formation degraded after the 1982 AT&T breakup and was suspended in 1987.
- S&P GMI revises its counts (2020: 630, later 518).
findings.confidence: verified-primary for the 2005 reform, D&B and net business formation items; secondary for the Subchapter V items (law-firm note) and the S&P revision

open_questions: P1. Get the postwar monthly D&B failure liabilities (BCD series 14, 1948-1989, from the FRASER BCD tables; annual Historical Statistics data to 1998). This is the only bankruptcy-related series with a documented leading record, and it needs a pre-registered out-of-sample re-test. It decides whether any bankruptcy series earns an alert.

P1. Find a modern size-weighted large-firm series with enough history. The S&P GMI tally appears to start in 2010 (start unconfirmed; site returned 403) and gets revised (2020: 630, later 518). The UCLA-LoPucki database (Oct 1979 to Dec 2022) is subscription-only and no longer updated. BankruptcyData is paywalled. Casey needs to decide whether to buy or obtain one of these; it decides whether that test is feasible.

P1. Status of S.3977 / H.R.7730, which would restore the $7.5M Subchapter V limit: enactment and any retroactivity. Either would create a jump in small-business Chapter 11 counts in late 2026 that any alert must flag.

P2. Primary confirmation of monthly default-rate peak dates for 2009 and 2020-21, and of the 2016 energy wave (currently press-only), plus access to the S&P or Fitch distress-ratio history to test the contested 6-12 month lead. This sets whether the distress ratio deserves a pre-registered test.

P2. Regional test, which would be new: US Courts filings by district or state and NY Fed state delinquency transition rates vs state payrolls or Philadelphia Fed state coincident indexes. Use Garrett & Wall-style trend and fixed-effect controls, and pre-register it, because the published evidence runs the other way (labor markets lead filings).

P2. Sources not read: the full text of Fay, Hurst & White (AER 2002, paywalled), the ABA Business Law Today 2022 piece on 2020-21 filings (403), the Guggenheim distress-ratio note (404), and S&P GMI articles (403). These could refine the strategic vs shock-driven filing picture and the practitioner claims.

P3. The claim that charge-offs lag was not verified from primary literature in this pass. It can be tested directly on FRED charge-off data (CORCCACBS) vs delinquency rates (DRCCLACBS) around 1990, 2001, 2008 and 2020.

P3. The specifics of the Conference Board's 1996 revision were not opened. The verified facts are that the 1989 revision added no failure series and that today's leading index and Leading Credit Index contain none.

verification.verdict:
The strand passes, but three issues must be fixed before the summary ships. It is genuinely sourced: every PDF and CSV it used is byte-identical to my fresh downloads (7 NBER chapters, 12 NBER working papers, Moody's 1920-2006, the NY Fed HHDC xlsx and the FRED CSVs). All 434 sha256s in MANIFEST.md match the files on disk, with no unlisted files. The classic lead/lag numbers check out to the decimal (Mitchell-Burns 1938, Moore 1950, Zarnowitz-Lerner 1961, Moore-Shiskin 1967, Zarnowitz 1992). Nothing is fabricated, and unverified items are labelled as such.

The three blocking issues:
1. The legal-break list is stale and incomplete. H.R. 7730 has passed both chambers and gone to the President, according to the very Epiq release the strand cites. The bill also raises the Chapter 13 debt limit, which the strand omits.
2. Open question P1 asks Casey to buy a size-weighted large-firm series. That is wrong: the FJC IDB has free case-level liabilities from FY2008, and LoPucki is no longer sold.
3. The conclusion that the leading signals are "already mostly on the dashboard" is overstated. It also omits WARN advance-layoff notices, which have a documented short lead over claims and unemployment.

Material corrections:
- Filings did NOT fall in the 2001 or 1981-82 recessions. The AO data frozen in the repo show +19% in 2001 and business filings +44% in 1982; only 2020 fell.
- Failure counts LED at business-cycle peaks (-5.0 months on average, unreliably). They were not coincident.
- Zarnowitz-Lerner's "large firms turn first" result holds at troughs. At peaks, large-firm series were more consistent but not earlier.
- Default rates before 2020 were rising and above their long-run average, not near record lows.

The core bottom line survives: do not alert on total filings. Dollar-weighted failure liabilities are the only bankruptcy-type series with a historical lead, and that lead is erratic and failed after 1948.
blocking: LEGAL BREAKS ARE STALE AND INCOMPLETE. The strand says H.R.7730 'left committee in March 2026' and that enactment is unconfirmed, and it flags only the Subchapter V change. The release the strand itself cites (Epiq, Oct 8 2026; reprinted by ABF Journal Oct 9) says H.R. 7730 'passed the Senate on September 28' and 'has been sent to the president for signature'. ABI says the House passed it on Sept 16. Corrected: the bill permanently restores the Subchapter V debt limit to $7.5M AND raises the Chapter 13 debt limit to $2.75M, removing the secured/unsecured distinction. That is a second break, hitting individual Chapter 13 counts (about 36% of 2026 YTD individual filings; individual filings are about 95% of the total). Signature, effective date and retroactivity are unconfirmed as of 2026-10-12. Every filings panel or alert from Q4 2026 must carry break flags for small-business Chapter 11/Subchapter V AND for Chapter 13 (and the Ch7/Ch13 mix). P1 narrows to: signed? effective when? retroactive? Evidence: epiqglobal.com 'Small Business Subchapter V Elections Increase 46%...'; abi.org/node/1004060.

P1 ('Casey must buy or obtain S&P GMI, LoPucki or BankruptcyData; this decides whether the size-weighted test is feasible') IS WRONG. (a) The FJC Integrated Database is free and openly downloadable (2.36 GB). It is case-level: filing date, district and county, chapter, Subchapter V and small-business flags, estimated asset/liability ranges, and scheduled TOTASSTS/TOTLBLTS. It runs from FY2008 (Oct 2007) to the 2026-06-30 snapshot, posted 2026-09-02, so the lag is about 2 months. It supports a liabilities-weighted or large-case Chapter 11 series for 2007-2026 at no cost, and it is already recorded in the study's own MANIFEST.md. Limits: no NAICS field, and only two recessions in the window. (b) The LoPucki BRD is NOT for sale. Its site says it stopped updating after Jan 2023 and 'will no longer sell copies or subscriptions'. A free copy can be downloaded, but its terms restrict use to academic research, so this is a licence question for Casey, not a purchase. It holds 1,218 cases through Dec 2022 (about 28 a year). Only S&P GMI (history from about 2010, and revised) and BankruptcyData remain paid.

THE 'LEADING SIGNALS ARE ALREADY MOSTLY ON THE DASHBOARD' CONCLUSION (#4) IS OVERSTATED, AND THE STRAND OMITS THE MOST DIRECT 'SOMEONE ELSE IS ABOUT TO LOSE INCOME' SIGNAL. Per the dashboard context, stock drawdowns and volatility, credit-market sentiment (Lopez-Salido, Stein & Zakrajsek) and household-debt growth are not on the dashboard. The excess bond premium is shown descriptively only, after the Aug-2026 referee rejected it out of sample. WARN Act advance-layoff notices are missing entirely. Krolikowski & Lunsford (Cleveland Fed WP 20-03; revised 20-03R, 2022) find that the number of workers in WARN notices leads state initial claims and changes in the unemployment rate and employment, strongest at 1-2 months. The 2022 version also finds they improve pseudo-real-time unemployment forecasts. State-level data are free on openICPSR (E155161), updated twice monthly. This adds a candidate, and a regional map, to the pre-registered test.

corrections.claim: Bottom line: filings 'fell during the 1981-82, 2001 and 2020 recessions' (relayed from Garrett & Wall: the rate 'actually fell' in '1982-83 and 2001').
corrections.problem: Contradicted by the AO filings data frozen in the repo, and by Eugeni (1991). The claim was passed on from the paper without checking it against the data.
corrections.correct_version:
Total filings rose in every recession since 1980 except 2020:
- 1981: +9.9%.
- 1982: total +4.5%, business +44.0%; only non-business filings dipped (-1.5%, after +9.8% in 1981).
- 1990: +15.2%; 1991: +20.6%.
- 2001: +19.0%. Non-business filings were up 16-25% y/y in every 2001 quarter; business +13.0%.
- 2008: +31.4%; 2009: +31.8% (partly the post-2005-reform rebound).
- 2020: -29.7%, from policy support.
Filings fell 5.0% in 2000, the year before the recession, so the rises are coincident, not leading. Filings are a coincident confirmer that failed once (2020); they are not a series that falls in recessions.
corrections.evidence: studies/distress_signals/data/derived/abi_annual_business_nonbusiness_1980_2025.csv and abi_quarterly_nonbusiness_by_chapter_1994_2025.csv (MANIFEST sha256 verified). Chicago Fed Letter 52: 'After increasing at the onset of the 1981-1982 recession, personal bankruptcy filings declined'.

corrections.claim: (a) Recessions (NBER peaks): 'Coincident: counts of failures'. Also: 'simple counts of failures, mostly small firms, moved roughly with the cycle'.
corrections.problem: The strand's own source (Zarnowitz-Lerner Table 12.2) shows counts LED at business-cycle peaks on average. They were coincident only at troughs.
corrections.correct_version:
At business-cycle peaks:
- All-firm failure counts led by -5.0 months on average: 8 leads, 1 coincidence, 5 lags in 14 turns (average deviation 6.8).
- Small-manufacturing counts led by -6.9 months.
At troughs, counts were roughly coincident (-0.5; trading-company counts +1.4). So at peaks counts are an unreliable lead, not a coincident series.
corrections.evidence: nber.org/system/files/chapters/c0732/c0732.pdf, Table 12.2 lines 9-12. Text: 'number of all failures and number of small manufacturing companies turn early at business cycle peaks only; at troughs, their timing is roughly coincident'.

corrections.claim: 'The lead comes from large firms' / 'Casey's instinct is right about the size-weighted, large-firm part', used as the basis for a large-firm RECESSION alert (alert idea #2).
corrections.problem: At peaks, which is the warning direction, Zarnowitz-Lerner's own numbers show the large-firm series were more consistent but NOT earlier. Their 'large firms first' evidence is at troughs.
corrections.correct_version:
At peaks:
- Large-manufacturing counts: -5.1 months (8 of 10 lead, 1 lag). Small-manufacturing counts: -6.9 (5 of 10, 2 lags).
- Large-manufacturing liabilities: -5.8 (9 of 10, 0 lags). Small: -7.9 (6 of 10, 1 lag).
In the direct large-vs-small comparison (Table 12.1B), large failures peak 6.4 months before small ones, which matters for revivals. At failure troughs (near business peaks) the two turn together (average 0). Z&L: 'At cyclical revivals, the lead in liabilities is due entirely to this factor.' Pre-register 'dollar-weighted liabilities vs counts' as the hypothesis, and test 'large firms turn first' rather than assume it.
corrections.evidence: c0732 Table 12.1 lines 7-8; Table 12.2 lines 3-6 and 11-14; pp. 353-359.

corrections.claim: Corporate default rates 'sat near record lows before 2008 and 2020'.
corrections.problem: True for 2008. Unsourced and wrong for 2020: the cited Moody's study ends in 2006.
corrections.correct_version:
Before 2008: Moody's global speculative-grade default rate was 1.57% in 2006, the lowest since 1981.
Before 2020: rates were rising and above the 1920-2006 mean of 2.69%. S&P's US speculative-grade rate went from 2.42% (2018) to 3.11% (2019), with 47 then 78 defaulters. Moody's global rate was 3.2% at end-2019.
The 2020 recession was an exogenous shock, so neither reading counts as evidence either way.
corrections.evidence: Moody's 1920-2006, Exhibit 21 (spec-grade mean 2.685). S&P 2019 annual US default study and Moody's end-2019 rate, via search snippets (S&P site returns 403), so secondary.

corrections.claim: Summary: after a liquidation, neighbours on the same Census block lose about 4% of jobs a year, 'mostly where the neighbours were already weak' (Bernstein et al.).
corrections.problem: Misattribution. The 'weak neighbours' result belongs to Benmelech et al. Bernstein compares liquidation with reorganization, not bankruptcy with no bankruptcy.
corrections.correct_version:
Bernstein et al.: conversion to Chapter 7 rather than Chapter 11 (instrumented by random judge assignment) cuts employment at other establishments on the same Census block by about 4% a year over 5 years (multiplier 1.3). The effect is concentrated in non-tradable and service sectors and in same-sector neighbours.
Benmelech et al.: closures concentrate among neighbouring stores whose parents are less profitable. At the 25th percentile of profitability they are 16.9-22.2% more likely to close; at the 75th there is no effect. Sample is 2005-2010, not 2005-09.
corrections.evidence: w23162 abstract and introduction. w20254 pp. 2 and 13 (0.36pp, 5.9% of the mean).

corrections.claim: 'Epiq's own head called filings largely a lagging economic indicator'.
corrections.problem: Misattributed.
corrections.correct_version: The phrase is Epiq's release text (May 7, 2020). Chris Kruse's own quote is: 'Unemployment claims historically correlate closely to bankruptcy filings, however, the speed of claims that occurred in April has thrown this correlation out of synchrony.'
corrections.evidence: Epiq release 'Bankruptcy Filings in April Down 39%' (epiqglobal.com).

corrections.claim: Consumer-bankruptcy debt relief 'raised employment by about 2% in 2007-10'.
corrections.problem: Presented as an estimate, but it is a model output.
corrections.correct_version: The reduced-form result is relative across states: more generous exemptions meant smaller non-tradable job losses (relative multiplier 1.81). The 'almost two percent' aggregate effect comes from a general-equilibrium model that requires substantial nominal rigidities and the zero lower bound.
corrections.evidence: w25685 abstract and pp. 3-4.

corrections.claim:
Dataset breaks for the D&B/NBER failure series:
- M0933A: 'Bradstreet vs Dun's coverage differences; Bradstreet's series ended Jan 1933'.
- BCD series 14: 'D&B coverage and definition changes'.
- Only M0933C is noted as not seasonally adjusted.
- Filing-series break list: 2005 reform, COVID, Subchapter V.
corrections.problem: Wrong or missing breaks that a re-test must handle.
corrections.correct_version:
M0933A is Dun's series, not Bradstreet's. FRED notes say its monthly data from 1894 include BANK failures, and a 1933 revision excluded real-estate and insurance brokers and holding and finance companies. Liabilities in the 1907 and 1930-33 bank-panic months are therefore contaminated.

All FRED NBER failure series are not seasonally adjusted, whereas NBER's timing work used adjusted data.

D&B moved to 'expanded coverage and new methodology' in 1984, 'not generally comparable' with earlier data, so any post-1966 test must split at 1984. The ERP series ends in 1997 ('Data are no longer published'). The HSUS Ch408-413 annual series runs 1857-1998.

Add the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978 (effective Oct 1, 1979) to the filing-series breaks. It inflates 1980-81, the pre-period for any 1981-82 test.
corrections.evidence: FRED series notes for M0933AUSM144NNBR and M0933CUSM144NNBR. data/dnb_erp/ERP-2004-table96.htm footnotes. w16872 (Richardson & Gou) cites HSUS 'Table Ch408-41: ...1857-1998'.

corrections.claim: P1: 'Get the postwar monthly D&B failure liabilities (BCD series 14, 1948-1989)... only as scanned PDF tables (needs OCR)', framed as a pre-registered out-of-sample re-test.
corrections.problem: It understates the data already in hand and mislabels part of the test window.
corrections.correct_version:
Already frozen in data/fred_nber:
- 1939-1968 monthly liabilities (M0933C).
- Postwar counts of large and small failures, 1948-69 (M09077/M09076).
- Failure liabilities divided by nonfinancial corporate current liabilities, 1946-69 (Q0983A/B). This scaling removes the uptrend Moore & Shiskin blamed.
The June 1987 BCD issue (Appendix C) prints series 14 monthly for 1953-1986 in a single table. It matches M0933C to the decimal for 1953-54 and 1966, so the OCR can be validated against FRED. 1987-88 are in the Jan 1989 BCD.
1948-66 is the period where Moore & Shiskin already found the series failing. The genuinely new evidence is 1967-1983 (4 peaks: 1969, 1973, 1980, 1981), plus 1984-97 on a non-comparable basis.
The strand's M0969B/M0971B files sit only in its scratch directory and are not frozen in the data directory.
corrections.evidence: MANIFEST rows for fred_nber/M09077USM234NNBR, Q0983AUSQ156NNBR and Q0983BUSQ156NNBR. FRASER BCD_061987.pdf Appendix C. BCD_011989 finding guide: 'Historical data (issue date) 6/87' for series 14.

corrections.claim: NY Fed new bankruptcy notations: 'peaked at 621 in 2010Q2'; '94-136 in 2020-22'; 2026Q2 is 'about 1/3 below the 2019 average'.
corrections.problem: The data are not seasonally adjusted, and the stated range is slightly off.
corrections.correct_version: Q2 is the seasonal high: 2019Q2 was 234 against a 2019 average of 204. On 4-quarter sums, consumer filings still peak after unemployment did: the AO non-business 4-quarter sum peaks in 2010Q3, against an Oct-2009 unemployment peak of 10.0%. The 2020Q2-2022Q4 range is 91-136 (2020Q1 was 189). 2026Q2 (136.8k) is 33% below the 2019 average but 42% below 2019Q2.
corrections.evidence: data/nyfed/HHD_C_Report_2026Q2.xlsx, sheet 'Page 17 Data' (sha ddfba16b...). data/derived/abi_quarterly_nonbusiness_by_chapter_1994_2025.csv. FRED UNRATE.

corrections.claim: 'Searches for state-panel causality or VAR tests of filings leading unemployment returned nothing.' The contagion section covers rivals, creditors, suppliers and neighbours.
corrections.problem: It misses one counter-citation and the direct channel to employees.
corrections.correct_version:
Hudson (1997, Applied Economics 29(5):647-654) reports significant Granger causality between company bankruptcies/births and output, unemployment, the balance of payments and inflation, in US and UK data. It is in-sample, and the abstract does not give the direction pair by pair. Cite it as weak supportive evidence for Casey's hypothesis.
Graham, Kim, Li & Qiu (JF 2023): employees of bankrupt firms lose 13% of earnings in the first full year after the filing, and lost earnings over 6 years have a present value of 87% of one year's pre-bankruptcy pay. Losses are worse in thin labour markets. This is the literal first-round 'someone else loses income' channel.
corrections.evidence: ideas.repec.org/a/taf/applec/v29y1997i5p647-654.html. nber.org/papers/w25922 (published-version figures via search snippet; secondary).

corrections.claim: 'Large-company filings have run at 16-year highs for about three years'; '785 large filings in 2025 per S&P... most since 828 in 2010' (sourced to Securitas); 'S&P GMI revises its counts (2020: 630, later 518)'.
corrections.problem: The cited source does not contain these numbers, and the revision claim may be a conflation.
corrections.correct_version: The Securitas page (Jul 15 2026) has only the H1 counts (372 in 2026 vs 371 in 2025). The 785 and 828 figures come from S&P's Jan-2026 release. 2024 was 687-694 (sources differ); each year since has been a post-2010 high, which is not the same as three years of '16-year highs'. The '2020 revised to 518' claim is unverified: 518 is also reported as the 2018 count. 2019 (579-589) was up from 2018, so large-firm filings were rising before 2020.
corrections.evidence: WebFetch of the Securitas page. Search snippets of S&P releases (S&P site returns 403).

corrections.claim: Minor accuracy items: (b) 'jobless claims lead (median 6 months)'; FDIC 2001 filings 'concentrated in telecom and energy'; net business formation entered 'the 1975 leading index'; Garrett & Wall '3,105 observations'; Epiq release 'Oct 9 2026' and September commercial Chapter 11 -16%; Jorion & Zhang 2007 '-0.41%'.
corrections.problem: Small misstatements, or claims that cannot be verified from the cited source.
corrections.correct_version:
- Claims' -6-month median lead is measured against NBER turns over 1945-61 (10 turns), not against unemployment. The repo's own Labor Stress Board finds claims rules confirm rather than lead.
- FDIC: 2001 public filings were 'distributed fairly evenly across industry sectors'. Telecom was 36 of 257 (14%) of the count; energy was 33% of assets.
- The net business formation index, which includes inverted failure counts, was in BOTH the 1966 and 1975 lists until it was suspended in Mar 1987. Failure liabilities left the short list in 1966 but stayed on the full list.
- Garrett & Wall's 67 quarters x 45 states = 3,015 (the paper's own arithmetic).
- The Epiq release is dated Oct 8; ABF Journal reprinted it Oct 9. The September commercial Chapter 11 drop of -16% is a base effect: Sep-2025 included 109 related filings by one pharmacy provider.
- The Jorion & Zhang 2007 '-0.41%' cannot be verified: the cited IDEAS page has no abstract.
corrections.evidence: c1270 table rows; fdic.gov FYI 013102; c10382 Table 11.5 (page image) and notes aa and k; MPRA 42740 p.~12; Epiq Oct 8 2026 release; ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v84y2007i3p860-883.html.

confirmed: Source integrity and data: every PDF and CSV the strand used is byte-identical to my re-downloads (NBER chapters c4251, c0726, c0727, c0732, c1270, c10381, c10382; NBER working papers w12362, w15848, w16685, w16872, w17021, w17830, w17854, w20254, w21581, w21879, w23162, w25685; the Moody's PDF; the NY Fed xlsx; the FRED CSVs). MANIFEST.md: 434 of 434 sha256s match, with no unlisted files.

Mitchell & Burns 1938: total liabilities of business failures are on the 21-series 'most trustworthy' list. Average lead 9 months at revivals only; 12 cycles and 14 revivals; 13 leads and 1 lag; range -17 to +6. Erratic movements 'pronounced'; a 6-month lag at the 1901 upturn. Bradstreet's series was discontinued in January 1933.

Moore 1950: failure liabilities are one of 8 leading series. Table 7.11 (Dun's, 1879-1938): peaks 14 turns, 11 leads, -10.5 months; troughs 16 turns, 14 leads, -7.5 (first line peaks, per footnote b). Table 7.1: peaks -23 to +2, average -8; May 1937 -4. Inverted liabilities peaked Apr 1945 (FRED M0933C minimum is 0.98 in Apr 1945), 43 months before Nov 1948.

Zarnowitz & Lerner 1961: Table 12.2 figures as quoted (liabilities -10.5 with average deviation 8.0, and -7.5; counts -5.0 with 5 lags, and -0.5; trading companies -0.4 and +1.4; large-manufacturing counts -5.1 and -6.9, anticipating 16 of 21 turns). Postwar leads of 28 months (July 1953) and 26 months (July 1957); 0 at the Apr 1958 trough; counts skipped 1953-54. Profit-diffusion indexes lead failure liabilities.

Moore & Shiskin 1967: series 14 scores 68 (conformity 86, timing 66, smoothness 0); 43 turns, 31 leads, 3 lags, median -7. 1960-list peaks -28 to +3; -12 at May 1960; no matching turn at Feb 1961. Dropped from the short list for 'poor timing and conformity record since 1948'. Initial claims: 73, 10 turns, 6 leads, 1 lag, -6. Instalment delinquency: 59, 8 turns, 6 leads, 2 lags, -3.

Zarnowitz 1992: Table 11.5 note aa (dropped 1966) and note k (net business formation suspended March 1987; AT&T breakup). Table 10.6: the 1950 leading group went from -6 to -12 months at peaks over 1948-75. BCD May 1975 confirms the net business formation index includes inverted business failures. BCD Jan 1989 still charts series 14 under 'Credit Difficulties'. The 1989 list and the Conference Board's six-component Leading Credit Index contain no failure series.

Garrett & Wall (Macroeconomic Dynamics 18(7), 2014): 45 states, 1988-2004; +6.4 and +12.4 above trend; peak about 6.8 in the second quarter of recovery; 12.6 of 31.6 points. National rate 0.3 to 1.2 per 1,000; 2.2 in 2005Q4 to 0.4 in 2006Q1. Cites Fay et al., White and Fisher.

Wang, Yang, Iverson & Jiang (Mar 2021): correlation 0.42 (0.54 excluding 2005), 'largely contemporaneous'. Filings -31%; Chapter 7 about -25%; Chapter 13 about -55%. Over 200k expected vs 81k fewer consumer filings; 5,500 expected vs 645 fewer business filings. States with bigger unemployment rises saw bigger filing declines.

Eugeni (Chicago Fed Letter 52, 1991): 'sometimes respond to recessions with a lag'; 'do not file for bankruptcy immediately'. Filings +20% in 1985 and +32% in 1986 (ABI non-business data: +19.9% and +31.6%). New England +65% in 1989-90. Epiq May 2020 release text: 'largely a lagging economic indicator'.

Giesecke, Longstaff, Schaefer & Strebulaev 2011: 13 default cycles vs 31 recessions; 3.2 vs 1.5 years; persistence 0.574 vs 0.267; correlation 0.263. Lagged spreads have no incremental forecasting power. Stock returns and volatility do predict defaults. The recession dummy is significant at 10% and drops out in the combined model. Spreads about 2x expected losses (about 80bp). Giesecke et al. 2014: default crises of 20-50% of bonds had little or no GDP/IP effect, and bank lending rose after them.

Moody's 1920-2006, Exhibit 21: 1986 5.64%; 1988-91 3.60, 5.80, 10.08, 10.40; 1998-2002 3.52, 5.83, 6.27, 10.59, 8.25; 2006 1.57%, the lowest since 1981. Conference Board EPWP 11-05: spreads 'lagging rather than leading... default rates, which tend to lag the business cycle'. Bond Vigilantes (Jan 16 2009): Moody's peak forecast went from 10% to 15.4%.

Gilchrist & Zakrajsek: about 3.0pp annualized lower IP growth over 3 months and over 1.25pp lower GDP growth over 4 quarters per 100bp. Baa-Aaa 'economically negligible' at one year. EBP 0.414 vs predicted spread 0.213 for 12-month unemployment; sample 1973:M1-2010:M9; in-sample. Lopez-Salido, Stein & Zakrajsek (1929-2013, sentiment at t-2), Mian, Sufi & Verner (30 countries, 1960-2012) and Lown, Morgan & Rohatgi ('four of the past five', exception 1981-82) as quoted.

Kiley (June 2022): 7 large-unemployment-increase episodes over 1965-2019. Composite leading indicators are useful up to about 12 months only. The corporate spread is insignificant at 8 quarters. Results are full-sample, not real time.

Mayer, Pence & Sherlund: trouble from mid-2005; serious delinquency averaged 1.7% over 1979-2006 and reached 4.5%; subprime 5.6% to over 21%; 1.2M foreclosure starts in H1 2008 (+79%). Liberty Street Economics (Aug 11 2026): 7.6% to 12.8%; 40% to 80% of charged-off debt still reported; flow 'relatively stable for almost two years'. HHDC 2026Q2: early transitions up slightly for auto and mortgages, steady for cards, serious unchanged; about 137k bankruptcy notations.

Contagion studies: Jorion & Zhang 2009: 251 Chapter 11 cases 1999-2005; creditors -0.90% (3 days) and -1.90% (11 days); industrial -2.29%, financial -0.34%; exposure about 0.3%. Lang & Stulz: -1% (abstract). Campbell, Hilscher & Szilagyi quote. Bernstein et al.: 4% a year, multiplier 1.3. Benmelech et al.: 0.36pp (5.9%) and 16.9-22.2%. Mian, Sufi & Trebbi: 20-30%, 15-25%, 20-35%. Mian & Sufi: about 4M of 6.2M jobs (65%).

Large-company filings: FDIC FYI (Jan 31 2002): 257 public-company filings in 2001 vs 176 in 2000 (+46%), running against the falling business-filing trend since about 1997. AP/BankruptcyData (Jan 13 2009): 136 in 2008 vs 78 in 2007 (+74%); record 263 in 2001.

Epiq release (Oct 8 2026), figures all match: 469,719 (+11%); individual 444,252 vs 399,379 is +11.2%, not the printed 7%; Chapter 7 282,413; Chapter 13 160,817; commercial 25,467; commercial Chapter 11 6,560; Subchapter V 2,442 (+46%); September commercial Chapter 11 648. S.3977 passed the Senate by unanimous consent on Aug 3 2026. The Subchapter V limit is $3,424,000.

FRED segment dates and units are as stated: M0933A 1894-01 to 1938-08; M0933B 1934-06 to 1939-12; M0933C 1939-01 to 1968-01; M0929C 1939-01 to 1965-06; M0969B 1934-06 to 1962-10; M0971B 1934-06 to 1961-02. Units are $mn or counts; all NSA. The 1939-40 coverage expansion is confirmed by FRED notes. Postwar 12-month averages show the strong uptrend.

Other items checked: the NBER's latest peak is Feb 2020 (BCDC page). Fay, Hurst & White is AER 2002, 92(3):706-718. HSUS Ch408-413 runs 1857-1998 (via Richardson & Gou 2011). FTI (Eisenband, Apr 4 2024): distress ratio moves 'in tandem... without an obvious lead-lag relationship'; correlation 'has broken down'; ratio about 6%; widest gap in 25 years; LTM measurement distorts lead/lag.

research.summary:
The data can support the study. The constraint is history: only a handful of recessions to test against.

**What was downloaded**
- 434 files (35 MB) went to /home/user/uranium-dashboard/treasury-canary/studies/distress_signals/data/.
- MANIFEST.md lists every file with source URL, retrieval date (2026-10-12), sha256, row count, date range and notes. MANIFEST.csv holds the same table in machine-readable form.
- Nothing is committed yet. The directory is untracked.

**Coverage**
- **Bankruptcy filings (US Courts Table F-2):** business vs non-business, by chapter, for 93–94 districts.
  - Quarterly 2001Q1–2026Q2; monthly 2013-01–2026-06; county-level (Table F-5A) annual 2013–2025 plus the 12 months to June 2026.
  - All 366 tables parsed and tie out: district rows sum to the national total, business + non-business = total, and monthly tables sum to quarterly.
  - Quarterly business totals match the American Bankruptcy Institute (ABI) series exactly in 100 of 100 overlapping quarters.
- **ABI compilations of court data:** quarterly business filings 1980Q1–2025Q4; quarterly non-business by chapter 1994Q1–2025Q4; annual 1980–2025.
- **Epiq AACER monthly** (the source behind the ZeroHedge headline): national commercial filings by chapter and filings by district, 2006-01 to 2022-03, from workbooks ABI posts.
  - After March 2022 only press-release text exists. 69 releases are archived.
  - The September 2026 figures were hand-checked. The headline +11% year-to-date total is correct. The release's "+7%" for individual filings is an arithmetic error; its own levels give +11.2%.
- **Dun & Bradstreet business failures:** monthly 1894–1968 (NBER, via FRED) and annual 1955–1997 (Economic Report of the President).
- **NY Fed household credit (Q2-2026 report):** new bankruptcy and foreclosure notations, flows into 30+/90+ delinquency, data 2003–2026.
- **Also downloaded:**
  - 26 FRED series of bank delinquency and charge-off rates, 1985/87/91 onward.
  - The Fed's GZ spread / excess bond premium CSV.
  - FDIC bank failures 1934–2026.
  - Test targets: recession dates, national and 51 state unemployment rates, jobless claims, Baa spreads, long equity indices.

**Not openly available**
- Moody's and S&P speculative-grade default rates.
- S&P Global Market Intelligence large-bankruptcy counts and sector splits (article text only).
- Industry/sector detail for business bankruptcies from any official source.
- Epiq data files after March 2022.
- Subchapter V counts, except in large court microdata or press releases.
- The LoPucki large-company bankruptcy database requires accepting academic-use-only terms. I did not accept them.

**Breaks any test must handle**
- 1978 Bankruptcy Code; 1984, 1986 (Chapter 12) and 1994 law changes.
- BAPCPA, October 2005: a rush to file, then a collapse and a permanent change in chapter mix.
- Subchapter V from February 2020, with its debt limit changing in 2020, 2022 and 2024.
- COVID support in 2020–21: filings fell while unemployment spiked. Student-loan delinquencies were hidden from credit reports 2020Q2–2024Q4.
- Dun & Bradstreet definition changes in 1933, 1934–39, 1940 and 1984.
- Bank data: the 2001 Call Report reform and the 2010Q1 accounting change for credit-card loans.
- Arkansas districts combined, and the F-2 table layout changed, in 2018Q3.
- The October 2025 shutdown: national and state unemployment are missing for that month.
- First-print court counts get revised up later (up to 5% for business Chapter 11 in 2008–09). Real-time tests must use first prints.

**Statistical power**
- Court data covers six recessions. The 1980 one has no lead-in data. In 2020 filings fell because of policy support.
- The Dun & Bradstreet monthly series adds 17 earlier recessions, but under a different bankruptcy law and definitions.

**Two side findings**
- The dashboard's "CRE delinquency" (backend/app/config.py:138 and severity.py:188) uses DRSREACBS. That series covers all real-estate-secured loans, residential mortgages included. Commercial real estate alone is DRCRELEXFACBS.
- FRED requests with cosd=1900-01-01 silently drop pre-1900 data. 14 series were truncated on my first pass. Use cosd=1700-01-01.

The Epiq '+7%' misprint and the DRSREACBS ('CRE delinquency') mislabel are real.

Blocking:
- **Regional history is missed.** ABI openly hosts AO district and state filings for 1980–2000, and quarterly consumer filings by district from 1996. The regional panel need not start in 2001.
- **Epiq Subchapter V comparisons are biased.** Each release revises the prior-year Subchapter V base down 5–11%. Headline growth is inflated: +46% as printed, +38% on first prints.
- **The BAPCPA break is mis-specified.** The chapter mix did not change permanently. The 2006–07 rebound overlaps the run-up to the 2008 recession and would create a false consumer-filing 'lead'.

Also wrong or missing:
- The first-print miss is one quarter at about 20–24% (2008Q2, led by Delaware), not 3–5% spread over several.
- The NY Fed panel and the bank-rate real-time vintages did not exist before about 2010–12.

That is true only of uscourts.gov. ABI hosts the AO's district and state tables as open HTML: annual business and consumer filings by district for 1980–84, 1985–89, 1990–94 and 1995–99; annual business filings by district 1990–2006; annual consumer filings by chapter at state level 1980–94; and quarterly consumer filings by district for 1996–97, 1998–2000, 2001–05 and 2006–11. Its United States row (331,264 / 43,694 / 287,570) equals ABI's national 1980 totals, and the 1990–94 page's 1990 row (782,960 / 64,853 / 718,107) also matches. With these tables, the regional panel can run annually from 1980, adding the 1981–82 and 1990–91 recessions plus the 1986 oil-patch, 1990–91 New England and 1991–93 California busts. EPIQ SUBCHAPTER V COMPARISONS MIX VINTAGES, AND THE BIAS RUNS ONE WAY. Each release quotes a prior-year base that has been revised down 5–11% since its first print. Jan–Sep 2025 was 1,764 (Oct-7-2025 release), now 1,672 (Oct-8-2026). H1-2025 was 1,183, now 1,107. Calendar 2024 was 2,381, now 2,202. Jan-2025 was 171, now 152. May-2025 was 228, now 207. Jul-2025 was 206, now 188. Sep-2025 was 210, now 200. Sources are epiq_press/…cleantext.json; I re-fetched the Oct-2025 and Oct-2026 pages live. Bases for total and commercial filings barely move (423,053 → 423,168; 23,666 → 23,789). So the strand's 'recomputed +46.1%' compares a 2026 first print with a revised 2025 base. First print against first print gives 2,442 / 1,764 = +38%. The Jan-2026 release's 'Subchapter V up 11% in 2025' is only +2.7% on first prints (2,446 vs 2,381). The strand's open question proposes transcribing Epiq release text into a series for alerting. Any such tracker must store each month's first print and compare like with like, or it will flag a spurious acceleration in the most alarming current reading.

THE BAPCPA BREAK IS MIS-SPECIFIED AND, AS WRITTEN, WOULD CREATE A FALSE LEAD BEFORE THE GFC. (a) 'Permanent change in chapter mix (Ch 7 80.0% in 2005 → 58.4% in 2006)' is wrong. The 80% was the rush to file before the law changed (85.6% in 2005Q4). Before the reform the consumer Chapter 7 share ran 68–72% (1994–2004). It returned to 71.4%, 71.6% and 70.3% in 2009–11, was about 70% in 2020–21 and 58% in 2022–23. The share is cyclical, not permanently shifted. (b) The rule 'never compute YoY changes across 2005–06' is too narrow. After the 2006Q1 trough, consumer filings rose from 112,685 to 218,428 by 2007Q4, and business filings from 4,086 to 7,985, all before the Dec-2007 peak. Year-on-year rises of 27–66% through 2007 are mechanical: the queue of filers who rushed in early in 2005 refilling. Consequence: for quarterly consumer filings, which start in 1994, the 2007–09 episode is not a clean test and 2020 is distorted by policy, so 2001 is the only clean recession. 'Six recessions' holds for business filings only. The study must exclude or explicitly model roughly 2005Q2–2008 for court counts, not just the 2005–06 YoY window.

research.summary:
Primary source: the Epiq AACER/ABI release of 8 Oct 2026. ZeroHedge relays an Epoch Times piece, which relays that release. The "11%" is correct for TOTAL filings, Jan–Sep 2026: 469,719 vs 423,168 (+11.0%). Individual filings also rose 11.2% (444,252 vs 399,379); the release misprints this as "7%". Other Jan–Sep lines: Ch7 282,413 (+13.4%), Ch13 160,817 (+7.7%), commercial 25,467 (+7.1%), commercial Ch11 6,560 (+11.3%), Subchapter V 2,442 (+46.1%; +38% against the 2025 base as first published, which was later revised down 5.2%). September alone: total 52,299 (+6.3%), individual 49,672 (+7.1%), commercial 2,627 (-6.9%), commercial Ch11 648 (-15.7%; -1.8% excluding one 109-affiliate case in Sep-2025), Subchapter V 276 (+38%).

Momentum is fading, not building. Year-over-year growth by quarter was Q1 +13.5%, Q2 +11.3%, Q3 +8.3%, with equal business days in each comparison. US Courts (AO) quarterly growth has ranged +9.6% to +20.3% since the upturn began in 2023, so Q3-2026 is likely the slowest quarter of the upturn.

Filings are rising from an unusually low base. AO filings for the 12 months to Jun-2026 were 608,511, or 1.78 per 1,000 people. That compares with 2.34 (2019), 5.12 (2010) and 6.99 (2005), and is below even the 2006 trough after the 2005 bankruptcy reform (2.06). In level terms it is 79% of 2019, 38% of 2010 and 29% of 2005; Jan–Sep is -19% vs 2019. The 2022 trough (1.14 per 1,000) is the lowest of 2001–2026.

Large corporates are elevated but flat:
- S&P Global Market Intelligence: 372 in H1-2026 vs 371 in H1-2025, the highest first half since 2010 (secondary source). Its Jul–Sep 2026 counts could not be obtained (spglobal.com returns 403).
- Cornerstone (companies over $100M of assets): 100 in the 12 months to Jun-2026, -15% year on year but +22% vs its 2005–2025 average.

Rated and private credit defaults are drifting up in H2: Moody's US speculative-grade default rate 5.3% in Aug (5.0% in Jun), with its Dec-2026 forecast raised to 4.3% from 3.5%. Fitch's US private-credit default rate is a record 6.3%. The high-yield spread is +45bp since 17 Sep.

Bank loan books (Fed data) are benign: delinquency on all loans 1.42%, the 8th percentile. Credit-bureau flows into 90+ day delinquency (NY Fed) are elevated for auto, 3.00% and the highest since 2010Q1, and for cards, 6.97%, above 2007Q4. Initial claims are 197k (2nd percentile since 1967), so the filing rise is happening WITHOUT a layoff channel so far.

Concentration:
- Regions: Sun Belt consumers lead (FL +21%, TX +21%, NC and SC +18%, MD +17%). TX and FL together supply 23.5% of the national rise vs 13.4% of the base. This is corroborated by ATTOM foreclosure data (worst rates SC, NV, FL, TX, MD) and the NY Fed (TX has the largest share of debt 90+ days late, 4.58%). The Midwest and Northeast are flat to low.
- Corporate sectors: industrials/manufacturing, healthcare, consumer discretionary, and finance/insurance/real estate (FIRE).

Measurement hazards are documented below:
- Epiq revisions and arithmetic errors in its releases.
- Clusters of affiliate (related) filings from single large cases.
- Large-case venue choice distorting district business counts.
- Epiq and AO definitions differ.
- A pending law change (H.R. 7730) that would break the Subchapter V and Ch13 series.
- The NY Fed's credit-report bankruptcy counts diverge from court filings.

Partial independent check: all 10 AO national totals and every Epiq Sep-2026 value match the data strand's own parse. The mandatory counter-agent review still has to run before anyone acts on these numbers. Scratch files are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-uranium-dashboard/2a5ba7c6-de7e-5470-a27d-d0386eb4bbf1/scratchpad/distress/current (current_state_readings.csv is the master table with sources).

- Subchapter V created Feb-2020; its debt limit fell from $7.5M to $3.424M in Jun-2024

verification.verdict:
PASS WITH CORRECTIONS: 3 blocking items, all about interpretation or omissions. I found no fabricated or wrong headline numbers. I re-opened every primary source and re-downloaded the files: Epiq releases (Jan–Oct 2026, Oct-2025, CY2025), the AO F-2 xlsx for Jun-2025 and Jun-2026, the uscourts release of 28 Jul 2026, FRED, the FRB charge-off pages, the NY Fed workbook, PDF, press release and Liberty Street Economics (LSE) post, the Cornerstone PDF, ATTOM, the First Trust and Fitch relays, and ZeroHedge. Every Epiq, AO, Fed, NY Fed, Cornerstone and ATTOM figure the strand quotes reproduces. My re-downloads of the NY Fed workbook, the AO xlsx and the Cornerstone PDF are byte-identical to the strand's copies. MANIFEST.csv: all 434 sha256 values match, and no files are unlisted. The problems:
- The regional-concentration claim is overstated and mis-corroborated.
- NY Fed measurement caveats are missing: 4-quarter moving sums, and a stock measure inflated by charged-off balances.
- The Subchapter V break list is incomplete.
- The upturn is misdated (it began 2022Q3, not 2023), so "slowest quarter of the upturn" is wrong.
- There are smaller attribution and staleness slips.
Scratch work: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-uranium-dashboard/2a5ba7c6-de7e-5470-a27d-d0386eb4bbf1/scratchpad/distress/verify-current (scripts/, dl/).
blocking:
REGIONAL CONCENTRATION IS OVERSTATED. 'Sun Belt leads; three independent sources agree' should not drive a regional panel or alert as written.
(a) The NY Fed support cited (TX 90+ share 4.58%, +0.65pp) is the STOCK measure. The NY Fed's own LSE post (11 Aug 2026) says this measure is inflated by charged-off balances, which now stay on credit reports about 80% of the time a year later, versus about 40% in 2004–12. The FLOW measures the NY Fed recommends fell year on year: TX 90+ transition 3.97→3.33, TX 30+ 6.87→6.59, FL 90+ 3.52→3.11 (HHDC pp.37–38).
(b) ATTOM's worst-rate states (NV, SC, FL) were the same in Aug-2025. FL's rate rose only 5% (1/2,512→1/2,397) against 12% nationally (1/3,987→1/3,569). ATTOM's H1-2026 top five includes IN, IL and DE, which contradicts 'Midwest flat'.
(c) The growth leaders are low-level states. Consumer filings per 1,000 people: TX 1.18, NC 0.93, SC 0.98, DC 0.81, US 1.70. The highest-rate states (AL 4.12, TN 3.06, NV 2.90, GA 2.87) grew at or below the national rate. AZ, AL, TN, LA, MS, NM and OK all grew below the 12.0% national rate; WV grew 17.0%.
The only corroboration that holds is NY Fed bankruptcy notations (4-quarter sums): TX +13.8%, FL +14.0% vs US +6.6%. NV leads that measure at +25.2%.
Fix: rank regions on per-capita level against each state's own history, plus flow measures. Do not use growth ranks or stock delinquency.

NY FED SERIES NEED PRE-REGISTERED MEASUREMENT RULES before any lead/lag test or alert.
- All flow and transition series (national HHDC pp.13–14, state pp.37–38) are 4-quarter moving sums, per the PDF chart notes and the LSE post. They are smoothed, carry a built-in lag of about 1.5 quarters, and overlap from quarter to quarter. The strand reports them as point-in-time quarterly readings ('auto highest since 2010Q1') without saying so.
- Stock 90+ series (pp.12, 35) drift upward for non-economic reasons. Nationally, the whole year-on-year rise in 90+ including derogatory balances (3.04%→3.31%, p.11) comes from the severely-derogatory bucket (1.51%→1.99%).
- Student-loan flows are broken from 2025Q1 by re-reporting (0.70% in 2024Q4, then 8.04%, peak 16.19%, now 7.83%).
Rule: flows only, align lags for the 4-quarter sum, mask student loans.

SUBCHAPTER V BREAK LIST IS INCOMPLETE, and the June 2024 level is misstated. The limit did not fall to $3.424M in Jun-2024. It reverted to $3,024,725 on 21 Jun 2024 and was indexed to $3,424,000 on 1 Apr 2025, which made about 13% more debt eligible.
That April 2025 step falls inside the Q1-2026 year-on-year window. Q1 growth was +67%, against +37% in Q2 (840 vs 615) and +42% in Q3 (812 vs 573), which are clean windows.
An alert must mask every break: Feb-2020 creation ($2.73M); Mar-2020 CARES ($7.5M); 27 Mar 2022 lapse; Jun-2022 restoration (partly retroactive); 21 Jun 2024 lapse; 1 Apr 2025 indexation; H.R. 7730 (pending). Chapter 13 limits moved on the same 2024 and 2025 dates.
Two further caveats on 'small business is the fastest-rising filer group':
- It counts Subchapter V elections, which substitute for regular Ch11. Total commercial filings were only +7.1% Jan–Sep and -6.9% in Sep.
- The 2026 monthly first prints sum to 2,492, versus the year-to-date print of 2,442.
